Dare means to have the courage or boldness to do something — especially something that feels risky, frightening, or socially forbidden.

The key thing to understand is this: you "dare" to do something only when there is some kind of resistance to overcome. That resistance could be fear, danger, social pressure, a rule, or the possibility of embarrassment. If something is perfectly comfortable and easy, you don't "dare" to do it — you simply do it.

  • "She dared to speak the truth in front of the whole crowd." (It took courage — most people would have stayed silent.)
  • "No one dared enter the abandoned house." (Fear was the resistance.)
  • "He didn't dare tell his father about the broken window." (Fear of consequences.)

1. To have the courage to do something yourself

This is the most common use. The subject of the verb is the person who must summon courage. The structure is:

dare + to + verb (or in certain grammar patterns, just dare + verb — more on this below)

  • "I didn't dare to ask her out." (I was too afraid.)
  • "She dared to challenge the unfair rule." (She was brave enough to do it.)
  • "Would you dare to walk alone at night in that area?" (Do you have the courage?)

Notice that "dare" in this sense always carries an undertone of overcoming something internal or external — a fear, a risk, a social norm.

2. To challenge someone to do something

Here, "dare" becomes a transitive verb — meaning it takes an object (a person). You are essentially testing someone's courage by issuing a challenge.

Structure: dare + someone + to + verb

  • "I dare you to jump into the cold water." (I'm challenging you — let's see if you're brave enough.)
  • "She dared him to ask the teacher a difficult question."
  • "They dared each other to eat the spiciest dish on the menu."

This is the same "dare" used in the popular children's game Truth or Dare, where a "dare" (used as a noun from the same word) means a challenge you must complete.

When you dare someone, there's often a taunting or provoking quality to it — you're saying, in effect, "I bet you won't."

3. "How dare you/he/she/they...?" — Expressing outrage

This is a fixed expression used to express strong moral indignation — the feeling that someone has done something completely unacceptable and shockingly bold.

  • "How dare you speak to me like that!" (You had the audacity — and I find it outrageous.)
  • "How dare he lie to her face after everything she did for him!"
  • "How dare they treat their employees this way?"

This isn't really a question expecting an answer. It's an expression of anger mixed with disbelief. The feeling behind it is: "What gave you the nerve to do that?"
A Special Note on Grammar: "Dare" Behaves in Two Different Ways

This is something most learners don't know, and it's important.

"Dare" is unusual in English because it can work as two different types of verb — a regular verb and a modal verb (like can, must, should, will). Both are correct. They express the same idea but follow different grammar rules.

Dare as a regular verb (most common, especially in everyday speech)

When used as a regular verb:

  • It takes "to" before the next verb
  • It gets -s in the third person singular (he/she/it dares)
  • Questions and negatives use do/does/did

Examples:

  • "She dares to speak her mind." (third person, present)
  • "Does he dare to challenge the decision?"
  • "I didn't dare to look at him."
  • "They don't dare to complain openly."

Dare as a modal verb (more formal; common in British English and literary writing)

When used as a modal verb:

  • No "to" before the next verb
  • No -s in the third person singular (she dare not — never "she dares not" in this pattern)
  • No do/does/did — instead, "dare not" or the contraction "daren't" is used directly

Examples:

  • "I dare not tell him." (= I don't dare to tell him)
  • "She dare not speak." (not "she dares not" in this modal pattern)
  • "Dare he say that to her face?" (question, no "does")
  • "He daren't look at her." (contraction of "dare not")

Quick way to remember: The modal form feels a little more old-fashioned, literary, or formal. You'll see it in novels, formal speeches, or British English more often. In everyday American English, the regular verb form is far more common.
The Fixed Phrase: "I dare say" / "I daresay"

This is a fixed expression worth knowing. "I dare say" (also written as one word: I daresay) does not mean courage. It means "I suppose," "I think it's likely," or "I imagine."

  • "I daresay he'll be late, as always." (I suppose / I'd guess he'll be late.)
  • "I dare say you're right about that." (I think you probably are.)

This phrase is somewhat old-fashioned and more common in British English, but you'll still encounter it in books and formal writing.

To truly understand "dare," feel the emotional texture of it:

Daring is not recklessness. It is not stupidity. It is not aggression. It is the act of consciously choosing to do something despite the fear, the risk, or the social pressure not to do it. There is always a moment of hesitation before daring — and then a decision to move forward anyway.

This is why we call bold, adventurous, or courageous people "daring" (the adjective), and why we call courageous actions "dares" (the noun).

  • "That was a daring rescue." (Brave, done despite serious risk.)
  • "She has a daring personality." (She goes where others fear to go.)
  • "Jumping off that cliff was quite a dare." (A bold, risky challenge.)
